caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Uruguay's debt is elevated but has never been explosive - the concern is drift, not crisis. It fell from 61.1% of GDP in 2006 to 40.9% in 2010 on the commodity boom, then rose in most years after: 49.8% in 2012, 57.8% in 2015, 59.6% in 2019, and 68.2% in 2020 on COVID, the series high. Recovery brought it down to 59.4% in 2022 before it climbed again to 63% in 2023, 67.6% in 2024, and a projected 65.7% in 2025. The drivers are persistent primary deficits and a large share of dollar-denominated debt that punishes peso weakness. Dollar GDP grew from $21.4bn in 2006 to a projected $85.6bn in 2025, which has kept the ratio bounded. A 2020 fiscal rule (expenditure ceiling) was meant to anchor consolidation, but compliance has been uneven and the new Broad Front government faces pressure to spend.
inflation_management: Uruguay runs one of the region's longest-standing inflation-targeting regimes (since 2007), but for most of the period it missed its own band from above. Inflation ran 6.4-8.9% from 2006 through 2015, hit a series high of 9.6% in 2016, then 6.2-7.9% in 2017-2019, 9.8% in 2020, 7.7% in 2021, and 9.1% in 2022. The central bank's contractive stance from 2021 - holding rates high through the global shock - finally broke the pattern: inflation fell to 5.9% in 2023, 4.8% in 2024, and a projected 4.7% in 2025, inside the target range for the first sustained period in the dataset. The achievement is real but fragile: Uruguay's inflation has a history of re-accelerating whenever the peso slides or wage indexation feeds through.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; Uruguay's banking buffers limited the damage.
Commodity boom peaked; debt began its long drift upward.
Luis Lacalle Pou won (Nov 2019), ending 15 years of Broad Front rule; took office March 2020.
COVID-19; the LUC omnibus law reshaped security, education, and labor rules.
Historic drought - among the worst in a century - hit soy and agriculture.
Inflation fell inside the target band for the first time in the series (4.8%).
Yamandu Orsi (Broad Front) won the Nov 24, 2024 runoff; inaugurated March 1, 2025; debt projected at 65.7%.

outlook_next_decade: Uruguay's base case is continued stability with modest growth: inflation inside target, investment-grade institutions, and a new left government that has so far signaled pragmatism over ideology. The structural challenge is the debt drift - 65.7% of GDP and rising slowly in a country that cannot afford complacency given its dollarized liabilities. Upside comes from green hydrogen, tech services, and deeper Mercosur integration; the risk is that social spending pressures under Orsi erode the fiscal rule and reopen the inflation cycle of 2006-2022. This is a well-managed economy whose main enemy is its own gradualism.
